editorial:
Abel Gance shot J'accuse! for PathÃ© FrÃ¨res across 1918 and 1919, filming parts of the climactic 'return of the dead' sequence with soldiers on furlough from the Western Front â€” men who returned to combat at Verdun shortly after the cameras stopped. The 166-minute film was among the most ambitious French productions of its era, screened widely across Europe and distributed in the United States through PathÃ© Exchange. Its US copyright â€” whether registered at the time or not â€” expired no later than 1975 under the 1909 Act's 56-year ceiling; even under a URAA restoration scenario (restoration in 1996 for a film never US-registered), a 95-year term from 1919 publication would have ended January 1, 2015. The underlying footage â€” battlefield tableau, double-exposure ghost sequences, and antiwar intertitles â€” is unencumbered for documentary, remix, or theatrical use.

The rights trap is the score. Lobster Films (Paris) and the Netherlands Filmmuseum assembled surviving prints from three countries and released a restored edition on DVD in 2008 with a newly commissioned score by composer Robert Israel. That score is a 2008 copyrighted work; any version of the film carrying it â€” including an Archive.org upload explicitly labeled 'restored' â€” has a protected audio track that cannot be reused without a Lobster Films license. Reusers sourcing footage should confirm they are working from a silent print and supply their own musical accompaniment, or negotiate directly with Lobster Films for the full restoration.
faq: Is the J'accuse! (1919) film in the public domain in the US?

The underlying film â€” its footage, cinematography, and intertitles â€” is in the public domain in the US. The maximum US copyright term for a 1919 work (28 years plus one 28-year renewal) expired no later than 1975, and even the outer URAA scenario (a 95-year restored term from 1919) would have ended January 1, 2015. The print is free to use. However, modern-restoration copies carry a separately copyrighted score; confirm which layer you are working with before publishing.
Can I use the Lobster Films restored version of J'accuse!?

Not freely. The 2008 Lobster Films / Netherlands Filmmuseum restoration is a separately copyrighted work, and the Robert Israel score recorded for it is independently protected. If you find a copy online labeled 'restored' or carrying a named musical score, treat the audio as restricted. Use a silent print from the Internet Archive and add your own accompaniment, or contact Lobster Films for a license to the full restoration.
